chapter: Pianists, Basie, Lil Armstrong and closing
title: Fats Waller as pianist and composer
summary: They call Fats Waller a great stride pianist and songwriter, and DeMichael wants a Fats Waller concert.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Fats Waller had a great, great gift that very few of the great musicians have. And that is, he got across to people who knew nothing about music.
Yeah, right.
I've had at least two people that I've known over the years who knew nothing about music, really. But were taken with Fats Waller. They both used to hear him, and they would go --
Right. Well, he was an entertainer.
But they'd talk about his piano playing.
But, I mean, he was an entertainer

but he was a combination. He was a great piano player. He was the daddy of the stride piano. You know the stride piano, where they -- he was the daddy of the stride piano. Him and guys like James P. Johnson and all those guys.
Yeah, and Eagle Eye [Shields].
Right, right.
That came out of ragtime.

Right, right, right, right, right, see, but it worked so good when these small combinations didn't have a bass player, see, because he was making these things, and Fats was a great piano player. And then, he played organ here at the Regal Theatre for a long time, over the years.
Pipe organ.
Yeah, right, he played -- oh, he was a great musician. And he wrote all of those tremendous songs, man.
You could do a whole evening of him.
Right, right, of Fats Waller. And then it's too bad, I mean, the people are not too hip to his tunes, his music. The musicians are, the older musicians, but, I mean, more the later musicians.
Yeah. One of the ideas I have for a concert at the Institute is to do a Fats Waller evening.
An evening of Fats Waller.
Yeah, and get a little band like he had.
Right, and the things like 'Honeysuckle Rose' and 'My Fate Is In Your Hands,' and --
And they say that he dashed those off --
Right, just like nothing, just like nothing. And then, Connie's Hot Chocolates, he wrote the whole show for that.
I was talking to Edith Wilson about that show, Louis Armstrong and Fats and she said they did a -- they were called the Three Tons of Rhythm or something, and they did some tunes.
Right, right, right, right.
